title: Trump Reimposed the Full Iran Blockade and Gave Tehran One Week. Power Plants and Bridges Are Next.
excerpt: The U.S. president threatened to destroy all of Iran's power infrastructure starting next week and refused to rule out a ground invasion of Kharg Island. Oil is at $85. Nine million Indians in the Gulf are in the firing line.
body:
The United States reimposed a full naval blockade on all Iranian ports on Tuesday, the most sweeping maritime action since the war began in February, as President Donald Trump threatened to strike Iran's power plants and bridges starting next week unless Tehran returns to the negotiating table.

The blockade, which took effect at 4 p.m. ET, covers the entire Iranian coastline — ports, oil terminals and coastal areas — and applies to all vessel traffic regardless of flag. Humanitarian shipments will be permitted subject to inspection, but the message from Washington is unmistakable: Iran's maritime economy is being severed again, barely weeks after the June ceasefire lifted the last blockade.

More than 20 U.S. Navy warships and hundreds of military aircraft are now deployed across the region, the Pentagon confirmed.

## 'Next Week Comes the Power Plants'

In an interview with Fox News that aired Tuesday evening, Trump laid out a week-by-week escalation ladder that goes beyond anything he has publicly committed to since the war began.

"We're going to hit them very hard tonight. We're going to hit them very hard tomorrow night. We're going to hit them very hard the night after," Trump said. "And then next week it gets really bad for them because next week comes the power plants. Next week comes the bridges."

"We're going to knock out all their power plants. We're going to knock out all their bridges unless they get to the table and negotiate," he said.

Trump compared Iran to "a great boxer" who still has "some fight left" but not much, and said U.S. strikes would continue "until I say that's enough."

The threats echo similar language from earlier in the conflict — Trump declared April 7 would be "plant day" and threatened energy assets again on April 19 — but neither deadline resulted in infrastructure strikes. Whether this round proves different could depend on Iran's next move.

## Ground Invasion of Kharg Island 'Not Off the Table'

Asked whether he would order a limited ground invasion of Kharg Island — a five-mile-long limestone island in the Persian Gulf through which roughly 90 percent of Iran's crude oil exports flow — Trump did not rule it out.

"I think it's unlikely," he told Fox News. "If we degrade them far enough and deep enough back, I would do that."

He added that any ground campaign would likely not involve U.S. troops directly. "Sometimes you need a ground campaign, but we have other people that will do the ground campaign for us," he said, without specifying who those partners would be.

Military analysts have warned that any assault on the heavily fortified, IRGC-controlled island would be extremely costly. The 82nd Airborne Division is on standby in the region, but experts say even an airborne operation would expose forces to Iranian hypersonic missiles and drone swarms from the mainland.

For the roughly 22,000 residents of Kharg Island, the threat is personal. "This is our home and our soil," one boat captain told The Times of London. "If they threaten us, why should we let ships pass?"

## Iran's Defiant Response

Tehran has shown no sign of bending. Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a televised statement on Tuesday: "If the U.S. thinks that by tightening its measures against us, its military actions and its economic blockade, we will return to negotiations, it is making a mistake."

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps announced retaliatory strikes against U.S. facilities in Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan on Tuesday, and issued a stark warning: "As long as U.S. forces remain in the region, no oil or gas will be exported — and the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed."

Iran's army confirmed early Wednesday that it launched drone attacks against the U.S. position at Jordan's Azraq base.

## Oil Surges, and Nine Million Indians Are Caught in the Crossfire

Brent crude has jumped 15 percent over the past seven days to $85 a barrel, the highest since mid-June. The International Monetary Fund warned last month that extending the war beyond mid-July poses "big risks" for the global economy, especially since countries have largely depleted their strategic oil reserves.

For India, the stakes are acute. An Indian crew member was killed and six others wounded when Iranian cruise missiles struck two Emirati oil tankers — the VLCCs Mombasa B and Al Bahyah — in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday. India's foreign ministry summoned Iran's deputy ambassador to lodge a "strong protest," noting that 30 of the 46 crew members on the two vessels were Indian nationals.

Another Indian national remains missing after an earlier attack on the container ship GFS Galaxy.

An estimated nine million Indians live and work across the Gulf states now under direct threat — Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman and the UAE have all come under Iranian fire in the past week. The conflict is no longer a distant geopolitical story for the diaspora; it is arriving at their doorstep.

India's oil import bill, already strained by a widening trade deficit that blew past $30 billion in June, faces further pressure as crude prices climb. For NRI families sending remittances home, a weaker rupee and higher energy costs mean less purchasing power on both ends of the wire.

The memorandum of understanding signed between the U.S. and Iran in June — the fragile ceasefire that briefly reopened the strait — now appears dead. Both sides blame the other for violating its terms. The question is no longer whether the war will end, but how much worse it gets before either side blinks.

*Sources: Reuters, Fox News, The Washington Examiner, The New York Post, CNN, The Wall Street Journal, The Times of London*
